strengths: Large-scale multi-organ ultrasound dataset from 15 hospitals (208,941 cases, 1.47M images) across 7 anatomical regions with careful data curation and filtering protocols
Comprehensive multi-task evaluation across report generation, diagnosis, and VQA tasks evaluated on seven anatomical regions
Ablation studies (Tables 5-7) systematically investigate MoE design choices including shared experts, routing strategies, and expert count
Supplementary analysis includes Grad-CAM visualizations, routing distribution analysis, and qualitative case studies providing interpretability
weaknesses: Unfair experimental comparisons: EchoVLM (11B parameters) compared against 7B baselines (57% larger); no same-sized baseline comparisons; incomplete training details for specialized baselines (LLaVA-OneVision-Ultrasound, Qwen2-VL-Ultrasound)

Critical evaluation methodology flaws: BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR scores don't measure clinical accuracy; no expert validation; no correlation between automatic metrics and medical correctness; entire evaluation relies on automatic metrics without radiologist assessment
Catastrophic failure on vessel imaging (BLEU-1 drops to 29.54 vs 43.50-50.76 for other organs) directly contradicts 'universal' claim in title; acknowledged but unresolved
Limited technical novelty: Standard MoE architecture, conventional two-stage training with LoRA, few-shot synthetic data generation—no significant methodological innovations for NLP venue

Data generation quality concerns: Only 5% expert sampling verification for synthetic data (insufficient); arbitrary deduplication thresholds; no comparison of synthetic vs. human-authored data; no analysis of diversity impact

Test set construction ambiguity: 3,000 reports with 27,577 images (~9 per report); image-report pairing procedure at inference unclear; potential data leakage not addressed
Weak VQA results: Model ranks second or lower in many metric-anatomy combinations (Table 4), suggesting architecture doesn't effectively transfer to all task types

strengths: Addresses genuine clinical need: ultrasound diagnosis is expertise-dependent with high subjectivity, making domain-specialized VLM valuable
Substantial dataset contribution: 208,941 clinical cases with 1.47M images across 7 anatomical regions from 15 hospitals with proper filtering and quality control
Methodical multi-task instruction-tuning pipeline: expert-defined templates, LLM generation with expert validation, ROUGE-L and Simhash deduplication with sampling verification
Comprehensive multi-task evaluation: report generation, diagnosis, and VQA across 7 anatomical regions with multiple metrics showing consistent improvements (e.g., +10.15 BLEU-1)
Thorough experimental work: detailed ablation studies (shared expert, Top-K routing, expert count), visualization with Grad-CAM, case studies across organs
Strong empirical results: achieves state-of-the-art BERTScores on most anatomies (heart: 89.80, kidney: 75.89) with clear methodology and implementation details
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: Mixture-of-Experts application is standard practice; 'Dual-path' design (frozen FFN + trainable experts) and two-stage training use well-established techniques without significant innovation

Critical absence of clinical validation: no radiologist evaluation of report quality, no comparison against clinical baselines, no quantified error analysis for safety-critical failures (acknowledged false negatives in nodule detection)

Inappropriate evaluation metrics for medical text: BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR are surface-level n-gram metrics unsuited for medical accuracy assessment; no medical-specific metrics or human evaluation by clinicians

Concerning generalization to minority classes: vessel imaging shows 21-point BLEU-1 gap vs. breast (29.54 vs. 50.76) despite acknowledged data imbalance; no concrete mitigation beyond mentioning rebalancing

Limited dataset generalization: all data from single region (China, 15 hospitals) with no cross-dataset evaluation; unclear generalization to different populations, ultrasound machines, and protocols; dataset unavailable for reproducibility

Incomplete architectural analysis: no study of expert specialization despite routing distribution figures; λ parameter never ablated; γ=0.001 chosen without sensitivity analysis; modest gains from 4-expert scaling question added complexity
Missing critical ablations: no analysis of instruction-tuning pipeline necessity, learning curves, data efficiency, or end-to-end vs. two-stage training comparison
Task definition ambiguities: unclear distinction between 'report generation' and 'diagnosis' tasks; VQA examples absent from main paper; mixed results on VQA (inconsistent baseline improvements)

Technical and reproducibility gaps: baseline fairness unclear regarding model capacity; training convergence behavior not discussed; hyperparameter sensitivity analysis missing; overclaimed 'universal' scope (only 7 organs)
Borderline venue fit for ACL: primarily a medical imaging application with limited NLP novelty; standard sequence-to-sequence generation without significant language understanding contribution

strengths: Comprehensive dataset contribution: Largest multi-organ ultrasound dataset (208,941 cases, 1.47M images, 7 systems) with thoughtful 'redefined desensitization' preserving clinical measurements and anatomical landmarks
Thorough experimental evaluation: Systematic comparisons against 12 baselines across 3 tasks with multiple metrics, ablation studies, entity-level evaluation, OOD testing, and case studies
Strong consistent empirical results: EchoVLM achieves SOTA across most anatomical systems (e.g., BLEU-1: 53.87, ROUGE-1: 61.69 average) with efficiency gains over full-parameter fine-tuning baselines
Well-designed architecture: Principled Dual-path MoE preserving base knowledge while learning domain-specific patterns through two-stage training with parameter isolation and LoRA
Reproducibility support: Detailed configuration tables, implementation details, promised open-source release, greedy decoding for determinism
Clinical relevance: Addresses genuine need for specialized ultrasound VLMs across 7 anatomical systems and multiple clinical tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: MoE application to medical VLMs is engineering-focused, not methodologically innovative; instruction-tuning pipeline builds directly on Self-Instruct; training strategy uses standard LoRA/MoE combinations

Clinical validity concerns: Acknowledges n-gram metrics (BLEU, ROUGE) correlate poorly with clinical correctness yet relies on them; no radiologist validation, inter-rater agreement, or clinical outcome studies; case studies show numerical discrepancies with ground truth not analyzed for clinical significance

Data quality validation gaps: Only 2.2% of 1.8M instruction pairs manually verified; LLM/VLM pre-screening may introduce correlated biases; 47% deduplication rate suggests potential diversity loss; no inter-annotator agreement metrics; desensitization approach privacy implications not addressed

Generalization issues: Poor vessel system performance acknowledged but not investigated or mitigated; limited OOD evaluation (only public KMVE dataset, no external institutions or rare diseases); overwhelming image-token dominance in routing suggests dataset imbalance

Incomplete methodological analysis: No ablation on desensitization approach; hyperparameter choices unjustified (γ=0.001 without sensitivity analysis, shared expert dimension 4× arbitrary); expert specialization analysis superficial; VQA underperformance vs. Lingshu unexplained
Venue fit gap: Fundamentally a medical domain-application paper with limited core NLP/computational linguistics methodological contributions; would be better suited for MIDL/TMI/JAMIA than ACL

Missing clinical deployment elements: No risk stratification, uncertainty quantification, fairness analysis across patient demographics, sensitivity/specificity analysis, radiologist usability study, or regulatory approval pathway discussed

Incomplete transparency: Minimal IRB details despite handling sensitive patient data; train/test split selection method unspecified; potential data leakage from using LLMs for both generation and evaluation; computational efficiency analysis absent (inference latency, throughput, memory footprint)
Statistical rigor: No confidence intervals or significance testing in results tables; case studies claim 'random selection' but limited to 6 anatomical systems due to space constraints

strengths: Substantial multi-organ ultrasound dataset from 15 hospitals with rigorous quality control and expert-validated desensitization preserving clinical information
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 tasks, 7 anatomical systems, multiple metrics including entity-level clinical evaluation and OOD generalization
Thoughtful expert-validated few-shot data generation pipeline with dual validation (AI pre-screening + manual expert review)
Systematic ablation studies on shared experts, top-K routing, and number of experts demonstrating architectural impact
Inclusion of entity-level metrics acknowledging imperfect correlation between BLEU/ROUGE and clinical correctness
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: standard MoE architecture with frozen+trainable experts is incremental; no novel routing, load-balancing, or sparse activation methods introduced
Unfair baseline comparisons: EchoVLM (11B) compared to 7B baselines with different training regimes; critically missing is EchoVLM (11B) vs. LoRA-only fine-tuning to isolate MoE benefit
Scope mismatch with ACL: primarily a medical imaging paper focused on ultrasound diagnosis, not an NLP contribution; better suited to MICCAI or medical AI venues
Absent clinical validation: no radiologist evaluation reported despite mention of expert verification; metric-to-clinical-utility gap unresolved; no error analysis of clinical failure modes
Unresolved critical weaknesses contradict 'universal' claims: vascular imaging shows 50% performance gap vs. best domains; VQA underperforms Lingshu baseline; issues acknowledged but not addressed
Reproducibility severely limited: data from private hospitals unlikely to be released; code availability incomplete ('available a'); 55.36 h/epoch training on 8×A100 high barrier to reproduction
Lack of evidence for MoE specialization: Figure 8 shows balanced routing across all experts; no demonstration that different anatomical domains activate different experts meaningfully

Data pipeline concerns: arbitrary deduplication thresholds (ROUGE-L >0.7, Simhash ≤3) lack justification; 47% data loss suggests substantial quality issues; diverse LLM ensemble may amplify rather than mitigate biases

Attention mechanism failures acknowledged but unaddressed: Figure 9 shows spurious attention to noisy regions alongside meaningful regions; critical for clinical imaging but treated as general VLM limitation

Incomplete experimental design: unclear patient-level train/test separation; no cross-validation or error bars; single train-test split without variance estimates; hyperparameter choices (LoRA rank=8, 4 experts, Top-2, γ=0.001) unjustified

strengths: Exceptionally large and rigorously curated multi-organ ultrasound dataset (208,941 cases, 1.47M images, 7 anatomical systems) with novel 'redefined desensitization' approach
Sophisticated expert-validated instruction-tuning pipeline with dual validation (AI + manual review), effective deduplication, and quality control reducing 3.42M to 1.8M high-quality pairs
Well-motivated and sound Dual-path MoE architecture that balances preservation of generic knowledge (frozen FFN) with domain knowledge injection (routing experts + shared expert)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 12 baselines, multiple metrics, 3 tasks, 7 anatomical systems, with fine-grained entity-level evaluation and OOD testing
Strong empirical results: 53.87 BLEU-1 and 61.69 ROUGE-1 in report generation (7.58 and 3.45 points over Qwen2-VL), SOTA across most anatomical systems
Thorough ablation studies on shared experts, Top-K routing, and expert count; clear reproducibility details (Table 9, Appendix B)
Practical clinical scope covering 100+ diseases across 7 major anatomical systems with multiple imaging modalities (2D B-mode, Color/Spectral/Tissue Doppler)
weaknesses: Critical absence of clinical validation: No evaluation by radiologists/clinicians on clinically meaningful metrics, no inter-rater agreement studies, and no assessment of clinical utility or workflow integration—a major gap for a medical AI paper

Significant dataset imbalance and representativeness issues: Long-tail distribution acknowledged but unresolved (Vessel only 2%), explicitly acknowledged 'suboptimal performance in vascular analysis' (BLEU-1 29.54 vs. 53.87 average), and geographic bias (all data from 15 Chinese hospitals) limit claimed universality
Weak performance on open-ended reasoning: EchoVLM underperforms Lingshu on VQA metrics, suggesting limitations in handling unstructured, open-ended tasks despite strong structured task performance

Spurious attention patterns concerning for clinical deployment: Grad-CAM visualization (Figure 9) shows model attends to irrelevant regions (image edges, black areas) alongside meaningful features; authors acknowledge but only suggest vague future work

Limited failure analysis and systematic error investigation: Case studies show successes but provide minimal analysis of failure modes; only brief mention of 'false negatives in nodule identification' without detailed investigation

Absent statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance testing, or error bars despite multiple comparisons and model size differences, making it unclear if improvements are statistically significant

Proprietary data limits reproducibility and adoption: Dataset not publicly available (understandable for privacy), code/weights promised but unavailable at review time, and high computational requirements (8×A100-80G, 55.36 h/epoch) further constrain reproducibility
Incomplete practical deployment analysis: Inference costs not discussed, latency not analyzed, and resource requirements for real-time clinical use unclear despite large 10B parameter model size

Moderate technical novelty: Dual-path MoE is incremental variation on existing MoE architectures; primary novelty is in application and data curation rather than fundamental NLP/architecture innovation
Limited domain-specific baseline comparisons: Comparisons primarily with general VLMs; few direct comparisons with other ultrasound-specific systems despite Table 1 cataloging related datasets
